content: 1. To identify target populations for tuberculosis preventive treatment (TPT), it is essential to establish a national technical working group or expand the mandate of an existing group. This group should advise the Ministry of Health and national tuberculosis (TB) and HIV programs. The working group should include national experts, stakeholders from TB, HIV, maternal and child health programs, patient representatives, civil society, frontline health providers, national research institutes, technical partners, and the World Health Organization (WHO). This group should lead efforts to identify target populations and develop strategies to reach them under the Preventive Management of Tuberculosis Preventive Treatment (PMTPT) framework. 2. The technical working group should review current national policies and guidelines for PMTPT. They should update these policies to align with the latest global guidelines, ensuring that the national approach reflects the most recent evidence and recommendations. 3. A situational assessment should be conducted to guide decisions on identifying target populations for PMTPT. This assessment should include: Evaluating the burden of TB disease and TB infection among various at-risk populations. Assessing the capacity of the existing health system, including staff, skills, and equipment, to evaluate TB exposure risk and exclude active TB disease. Reviewing the availability of financial resources and identifying gaps to support the nationwide scale-up of TPT services. Exploring opportunities to mobilize additional resources. 4. At a minimum, all countries should aim to achieve universal coverage of TPT among people living with HIV (PLHIV) and household contacts of TB patients under five years of age. 5. Other target populations should be identified through small-scale demonstration projects or phased implementation of PMTPT. These projects can help identify operational challenges and inform strategies to reach these populations with TPT services. Extensive research on the efficacy of TPT regimens is not required, as the WHO guidelines already incorporate in-depth reviews of clinical trial evidence. Delaying the scale-up of TPT services for additional studies risks denying vulnerable populations the benefits of TPT. 6. Specific populations, such as children, recent immigrants from high TB burden countries to low TB burden countries, individuals with recent contact with a TB patient, or those with documented conversion of TB infection tests from negative to positive, should be considered for TPT. For populations in congregate settings, it is critical to ensure effective implementation of TB surveillance, treatment, and infection control measures. Without robust airborne infection control measures, the benefits of TPT may be compromised due to the high risk of reinfection. 7. Ministries of Health, donors, and stakeholders should support capacity building to strengthen infection control measures and establish access to rapid TB diagnosis and treatment. Active case finding (ACF) linked to TB treatment and infection prevention is essential for scaling up TPT among at-risk populations, particularly in congregate settings. 8. All HIV testing and treatment facilities, including community-based HIV care and support services, should systematically implement intensified TB case finding, TPT, and TB infection control. This requires close collaboration between national TB and HIV programs. 9. All PLHIV should be screened for TB symptoms at every opportunity or during contact with a health worker. Those with symptoms should be referred for diagnostic testing, while those without symptoms should be evaluated for TPT eligibility and initiated on treatment as appropriate. 10. National TB and HIV programs should allocate resources and conduct site monitoring to ensure the implementation of TPT and address gaps, such as inadequate screening or lack of linkage to TPT. 11. For other target populations, national programs should tailor TB screening and TPT services to the needs and capacities of existing health infrastructures. The approach should aim to optimize and integrate TPT delivery with other health and social welfare services. Regular monitoring of target populations and screening approaches is necessary to improve service delivery. 12. Household contacts of TB patients are a well-recognized at-risk group for TB infection and disease. Systematic household contact investigation can detect new TB cases and identify individuals eligible for TPT. This approach is highly cost-effective and yields significant public health benefits by reducing TB transmission and improving outcomes for contacts. 13. Offering TPT to all family members simultaneously, while the index TB patient is still receiving treatment, can enhance the understanding and impact of TPT. It also improves cost-effectiveness by consolidating interventions such as home visits. 14. A strong contact investigation program is essential for achieving commitments to provide TPT to millions of household contacts. This requires investments to strengthen national program capacity, improve access to TPT, and identify missed TB patients for treatment, thereby reducing onward transmission. 15. Contact investigation should be a standard component of all national TB control efforts. It involves identifying, clinically evaluating, and providing appropriate anti-TB therapy or TPT to contacts of index TB patients. Ministries of Health should invest in strengthening health system capacity to undertake contact investigations effectively. 16. If mechanisms for contact investigation are lacking, the Ministry of Health should allocate necessary human and financial resources to establish effective systems. This includes providing standard guidance, defining roles and responsibilities, and ensuring respectful treatment and confidentiality during the process. 17. Contact investigation should prioritize household members but also consider workplace and other congregate settings where exposure is likely to have been prolonged. Maintaining confidentiality is critical to protect the social connections between index patients and their contacts. 18. Health providers should educate index patients and their household members about the benefits of TPT and the risks of not taking it. Counseling should enable informed decision-making and encourage the identification of all significant contacts to maximize preventive action. 19. Home visits provide an opportunity to assess the residence, counsel family members on TB symptoms, and link them to social and nutritional support programs. Prompt medical attention and referrals should be made for vulnerable contacts, such as children and PLHIV, who are at higher risk of rapid TB progression. 20. If home or workplace visits are not feasible, index patients should be interviewed at health facilities, and complete contact information should be collected for follow-up. Health workers should systematically mobilize contacts for TB screening, testing, and evaluation for TPT eligibility. 21. Integrating TB and HIV screening throughout the contact investigation process can enhance efficiency and sustainability. Ministries of Health should ensure that contact investigation programs are adequately resourced and supported to achieve their goals.
